analysis.one_liner: Bars federal agencies from issuing any rule or guidance that bans fracking nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill, which drew zero cosponsors, was introduced and placed on the Senate calendar but never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would prohibit any federal agency from proposing, implementing, or finalizing a rule or guidance that bans hydraulic fracturing — fracking — anywhere in the United States [S2] [S3]. No such federal ban existed or was pending at the time; the bill was a preemptive shield for the oil and gas industry against any future administration that might try to impose one [S3]. It did not change existing fracking regulation or permitting, which would continue unchanged [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, oil and gas producers and fracking service companies would gain the most: they would be legally shielded from any nationwide federal ban on fracking, no matter which party controlled the White House or what future evidence showed about fracking's effects on water, air, or earthquake risk [S2] [S3]. Drilling states like North Dakota, whose economies depend on fracking, would gain certainty that the practice stays available [S1].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas producers and fracking operators

how_it_helps.text: It would bar every federal agency from proposing, implementing, or finalizing any rule or guidance that bans hydraulic fracturing nationwide, removing the possibility of a federal ban regardless of future administrations or findings.
It would give oil and gas drillers and fracking-dependent states permanent certainty that fracking stays legal at the federal level, since only Congress — not an agency — could ever impose a ban.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would fall on people living near fracking operations who might want stronger federal protection from water contamination, air pollution, or induced earthquakes, and on future federal agencies, which would lose the option of a nationwide ban even if evidence later justified one. Taxpayers would bear no direct cost, since the bill changed no current program [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Residents near fracking sites; future regulators

drawbacks.text: It would have permanently tied the hands of federal agencies: they could not propose or finalize a nationwide fracking ban even if future evidence of water contamination, air pollution, or earthquake harm persuaded them one was needed.

It addressed a threat that did not exist — no federal agency had proposed banning fracking — and with zero cosponsors and no committee or floor action, its practical effect was symbolic rather than substantive.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered certainty to the oil and gas industry at almost no immediate cost, because no federal fracking ban was on the table. Its real cost was prospective: it would have foreclosed one policy option for the entire country, regardless of what future evidence or administrations concluded about fracking's risks. As a practical matter it was a messaging bill — it never advanced beyond being placed on the calendar [S5] [S4].

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar, but it never got a committee hearing or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Kevin Cramer introduced the bill on January 10, 2022; it was read a first time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar.
On January 18, 2022, it was read a second time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 239), meaning it sat ready in case the Senate chose to take it up.
No committee action, floor vote, or further action followed; the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died on the calendar.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing material changed: no federal fracking ban existed or was pending, so oil and gas producers kept operating under the same rules whether the bill lived or died. People who want the option of federal action on fracking lost nothing, because the bill was never close to passing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the status quo held

for.name: Sen. Kevin Cramer
for.role: U.S. Senator from North Dakota (bill sponsor)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and had it read twice and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote; it stayed on the calendar until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never came to a vote, so no roll-call shows the split; its only support was a single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Oil and gas drillers and fracking service companies
industries.note: The bill would have locked in fracking as the federally protected method for producing oil and gas, ruling out a nationwide ban no matter what future evidence or administrations concluded. No federal ban existed at the time, so its main function was to remove a future regulatory threat to the industry.

Fracking is the main method for extracting U.S. natural gas, so a federal fracking ban would have accelerated the shift away from gas; by taking that option off the table, the bill preserved natural gas's competitive position.
